name: Cheoyong
subtitle: The dancer who banished the plague.
shortDescription: A dragon king's son who, through his dance and song, warded off a plague demon from a Silla household.

description: Cheoyong is a figure from Korean mythology, best known for his role in expelling a plague demon during the reign of King Heongang of the Silla Dynasty. According to the Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), Cheoyong appeared as a man who danced and sang to drive away a demon who had taken the form of a man and slept with his wife. His image and story have been used throughout Korean history as a symbol of protection against evil spirits and disease. He is often depicted wearing the clothes of a government official and is associated with warding off illness and misfortune. The tale of Cheoyong highlights themes of resilience, resourcefulness, and the power of art in overcoming adversity. His dance became a ritualistic performance to protect against evil.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: The primary source for the Cheoyong narrative is the Samguk Yusa, compiled in the 13th century. The story recounts that during the reign of King Heongang, Cheoyong appeared before the king after the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea was pleased by the king's generosity. The Dragon King sent Cheoyong to the capital as a sign of gratitude. Cheoyong took a beautiful woman as his wife but one night, he returned home to find a demon disguised as a man sleeping with her. Instead of reacting with violence, Cheoyong sang a song and danced, causing the demon to reveal its true form and flee. This act of forbearance and the power of his dance became the foundation for his protective status.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Cheoyong's role in Korean culture is primarily as a guardian figure. His image is frequently displayed on gates and doors to ward off evil spirits and prevent the entry of disease. The Cheoyongmu, or Cheoyong dance, is a court dance that is performed to invoke his protective powers and purify spaces. The dance is characterized by its vibrant costumes, including a mask depicting Cheoyong with a dark face and wide eyes. The dance and image of Cheoyong are believed to possess apotropaic qualities, offering protection against misfortune and illness. His story emphasizes the importance of maintaining composure and using non-violent means to overcome adversity.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Cheoyong's story is rich in symbolism. His origin as the son of a dragon king connects him to water, a symbol of life, purification, and power. The demon represents disease and chaos, while Cheoyong's dance and song symbolize the power of art and culture to overcome these destructive forces. His act of forgiving the demon instead of resorting to violence can be interpreted as a message of restraint and the importance of maintaining moral integrity. The mask worn in the Cheoyongmu is also symbolic, with its exaggerated features and bright colors designed to frighten away evil spirits. The dance itself embodies a ritualistic cleansing, purging the space of negativity and creating an environment of protection and well-being.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Cheoyong's legacy continues to be felt in modern Korean culture. The Cheoyongmu remains a significant part of Korean performing arts and is recognized as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage. His image is still used in various forms of art and decoration, particularly during times of celebration or when protection is desired. The story of Cheoyong has also inspired contemporary adaptations in literature, film, and television, ensuring that his message of resilience and the power of art continues to resonate with new generations. The Cheoyongmu is still performed at important national events and festivals, solidifying his enduring presence in Korean cultural identity.
